## Title: Assessing Heat Vulnerability and Chronic Condition Prevalence in NYC: An Exploratory Analysis

Overview: This project explores the potential relationship between heat
vulnerability and chronic condition prevalence in the New York City
(NYC) area. The data come from the New York City Department of Health
and Mental Hygiene (NYC DOHMH) website and are publicly available for
download. In addition to exploring relationships between heat
vulnerability and chronic condition prevalence, this project also seeks
to identify potential community-level disparities that warrant further
consideration.

## Intro:

Heat exposure is a leading cause of weather-related deaths in the United
States \[3\]. Heat exposure is also quite common; more than two-thirds
of Americans were under heat alerts in 2023 \[4\]. Extreme heat is a
particularly serious environmental health risk to New York City (NYC)
residents. In fact, extreme heat is NYC's deadliest weather hazard,
taking more lives than hurricanes, floods, or winter storms \[10\].
Between 2018 and 2022, there were an average of 525 heat-related deaths
per year in NYC \[10\]. Most of these deaths occur in New Yorkers’ own
homes, often without air conditioning (AC) \[10\]. The risk is greatest
among communities already impacted by housing inequities, which
disproportionately affects black New Yorkers \[10\].

Approximately 100 heat-exacerbated deaths each year are attributable to
the most extreme heat days \[10\]. Extreme heat days are defined as days
that meet the extreme heat advisory threshold in NYC from the National
Weather Service \[10\]. The remaining heat-exacerbated deaths occurred
on non-extreme heat days, days below the heat advisory threshold but
above 82 degrees Fahrenheit \[10\]. Although these are not considered
extreme weather days, they remain dangerous; the number of these types
of days has increased more rapidly over the past decade than extreme
heat days \[10\]. Further, although non-extreme heat days have increased
rapidly, home AC rates have remained steady, suggesting AC access is not
keeping pace with rising demand \[10\]. This is dangerous because
without AC, indoor temperatures can become much hotter than outdoor
temperatures, especially at night, and can persist for days following a
heat wave \[10\].

Higher temperatures pose especially serious risks in NYC, where extreme
heat can exacerbate the urban heat island effect \[11\]. Buildings,
roads, and other infrastructure absorb and re-emit heat more than
natural landscapes such as forests and bodies of water; as a result,
urban areas become “islands” of higher temperatures relative to outlying
areas \[12\].

While heat exposure is clearly associated with a higher risk of heat
exhaustion and heat stroke \[5\], it also exacerbates multiple chronic
conditions \[6\]. People with chronic conditions may be more vulnerable
to heat because they have a reduced ability to sense and respond to
temperature changes and may take medications that worsen heat effects
\[6\]. Further, warmer weather traps greenhouse gases in the atmosphere
and worsens ozone levels, which can irritate lung tissue \[7\]. High
ozone levels or long-term exposure can worsen respiratory symptoms and
conditions, including asthma \[7\].

Similarly, extreme heat events often exacerbate diabetes-related
complications \[8\]. Diabetes can damage blood vessels and nerves,
reducing the body’s ability to cool itself effectively \[8\]. Further,
people with diabetes dehydrate more quickly, which is associated with
raised blood sugar, and high temperatures can change the way that the
body uses insulin \[8\].

Lastly, high temperatures and high humidity, in particular, affect
people managing hypertension. When exposed to high temperatures, the
body redirects blood flow to the skin to cool itself, which can raise
blood pressure and increase heart rate; dehydration from sweating also
reduces blood volume, further stressing the heart and potentially
raising blood pressure \[9\]. The combination of these two mechanisms
can exacerbate existing hypertension and put people at an increased risk
of experiencing heart failure, arrhythmias, or acute cardiac events
\[9\].

Using a health equity lens, this assessment will use epidemiologic
methods to characterize and analyze the relationship between heat
vulnerability, geography, and the prevalence of chronic conditions in
NYC.

## Methods/Results

Step 1: Download and Install Packages

```{r}
library(tidyverse) 
library(sf) 
library(tidycensus) 
library(janitor)
library(tmap) 
library(dplyr) 
library(readr)
```


Step 2: Load ZIP code geography

```{r}

zip_shapes \<-
st_read("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Modified_Zip_Code_Tabulation_Areas\_(MODZCTA)\_20260605.geojson")

```


Step 3: Load Heat Vulnerability Index (HVI)

```{r}

hvi \<-
read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv")

clean_names(hvi)

```


Step 4: Load Chronic Condition Data

```{r}

NEWasthma \<- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW Asthma
Dataset.xlsx - Sheet1.csv") NEWdiabetes \<-
read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW Diabetes Dataset.xlsx -
Sheet1.csv") NEWhypertension \<- read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/NEW
Hypertension Dataset.xlsx - Sheet1.csv")

```


Step 5: Merge chronic condition data

```{r}

chroncondition_data1 \<- NEWasthma %\>% left_join(NEWdiabetes, by = "Zip
Code") %\>% left_join(NEWhypertension, by= "Zip Code")

```


Step 6: Merge with HVI data

```{r}

hvi \<-
read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv")
%\>% clean_names()

hvi \<- hvi %\>% rename(zip_code = zip_code_tabulation_area_zcta_2020)

NEWasthma \<- NEWasthma %\>% clean_names() NEWdiabetes \<- NEWdiabetes
%\>% clean_names() NEWhypertension \<- NEWhypertension %\>%
clean_names()

chroncondition_data1 \<- NEWasthma %\>% left_join(NEWdiabetes, by =
"zip_code") %\>% left_join(NEWhypertension, by = "zip_code")

hvi \<-
read_csv("C:/Users/alyss/Downloads/Heat_Vulnerability_Index_Rankings_20260605.csv")
%\>% clean_names() %\>% rename(zip_code =
zip_code_tabulation_area_zcta_2020)

chroncondition_data1 \<- chroncondition_data1 %\>% mutate(zip_code =
as.character(zip_code))

hvi \<- hvi %\>% mutate(zip_code = as.character(zip_code))

NEWanalysis_data \<- chroncondition_data1 %\>% left_join(hvi, by =
"zip_code")


```


Step 7: check class

```{r}

class(NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y)
class(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)

```


Step 8: Run correlations

```{r}

HVI score v. asthma prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.x)

t-value= 2.4115

p-value= 0.0218 (statistically significant)

95% CI: 0.062-0.645

cor= 0.392 (weak/moderate linear relationship)

HVI score v. diabetes prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y)

t-value= 2.865

p-value= 0.000511 (very statistically significant)

95% CI: 0.279-0.758

cor= 0.564 (moderate linear relationship)

HVI score v. hypertension prevalence

cor.test(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence)

t-value= 2.9141

p-value= 0.006461 (very statistically significant)

95% CI: 0.142-0.689

cor= 0.457 (moderate linear relationship)



```


Step 9: Run SLR

CAVEAT: Only moderate linear relationships identified between HVI and
these 3 chronic conditions, so interpret cautiously

```{r}

SLRmodel \<-
lm(NEWanalysis_data$heat_vulnerability_index_hvi ~ NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.x +
NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence.y + NEWanalysis_data$estimated_prevalence)
summary(SLRmodel)

```


Under an SLR, none of the chronic conditions' prevalence were
significantly associated with HVI; however, asthma is on the border.
Weaker linear relationships between these two variables may be driving
these results

Findings: weak-moderate correlations between HVI and chronic conditions
and non-significant regression coefficients

Interpretation: Chronic condition prevalence ALONE does not strongly
track with HVI at the ZIP level. This makes sense because HVI includes
many components,

including housing quality, access to AC, green space, poverty, etc.
Chronic disease is just one piece of vulnerability.

## Now Re-framing as descriptive + stratified analysis

Step 1: Stratify ZIP codes by HVI

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data \<- NEWanalysis_data %\>% mutate(hvi_group=
ntile(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi, 4)) \# quartiles

```


Step 2: Compare chronic disease across groups

```{r}

NEWanalysis_data %\>% group_by(hvi_group) %\>% summarise( asthma=
mean(estimated_prevalence.x, na.rm= TRUE), diabetes=
mean(estimated_prevalence.y, na.rm= TRUE), htn=
mean(estimated_prevalence, na.rm= TRUE) )

```


Output/interpretation: Residents in the highest HVI quartile have a 6%
higher asthma prevalence compared to those in the lowest quartile.
Residents in the highest HVI quartile have an 8% higher diabetes
prevalence compared to those in the lowest quartile. Residents in the
highest HVI quartile have a 10% higher htn prevalence compared to those
in the lowest quartile

## Map it

```{r}

tm_shape(map_data) + tm_polygons( col = "burden_score", palette =
"RdYlBu", style = "quantile" ) + tm_layout( main.title = "Composite
Chronic Disease Burden" )

```


Create a composite chronic disease burden score and evaluate its
association with HVI.

1.  Create a composite burden score

```{r}

compositedata \<- NEWanalysis_data %\>% mutate( asthma_z =
as.numeric(scale(NEWasthma)), diabetes_z =
as.numeric(scale(NEWdiabetes)), hypertension_z =
as.numeric(scale(NEWhypertension)) )

```


2.  Create composite score

```{r}

data \<- compositedata %\>% mutate( burden_score = asthma_z +
diabetes_z + hypertension_z )

```


3.  Examine correlation with HVI

```{r}

cor.test( data$HVI,
  data$burden_score, method = "spearman" )

```


4.  Fit a SLR

```{r}

burden_model \<- lm( burden_score \~ HVI, data = data )

summary(burden_model)

```


5.  Create a scatterplot

```{r}

ggplot(data, aes(x = HVI, y = burden_score)) +

geom_jitter( width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6 ) +

geom_smooth( method = "lm", color = "red", se = TRUE ) +

labs( title = "Association Between HVI and Chronic Disease Burden", x =
"Heat Vulnerability Index", y = "Composite Chronic Disease Burden Score"
) +

theme_minimal()

```


6.  Compare mean burden across across HVI groups

```{r}

ggplot(data, aes( x = factor(HVI), y = burden_score )) +

geom_boxplot( fill = "lightblue" ) +

labs( title = "Composite Burden Score by HVI Category", x = "HVI
Category", y = "Burden Score" ) +

theme_minimal()

```


Another option: show concentration

```{r}

my_tibble \<- NEWanalysis_data %\>%
arrange(desc(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)) %\>% mutate(cum_pop=
row_number()/n(), cum_hvi=
cumsum(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi)/sum(heat_vulnerability_index_hvi))

print(my_tibble, n= Inf, width= Inf)

```
